summary: For ages 11–12, build understanding that white light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV ordered by frequency), that a prism disperses white light because different frequencies refract by different amounts (violet bends most, red least) and a second prism recombines it, that objects appear coloured by selective absorption and reflection (so a red object looks red in white light but near-black in pure blue light), and that filters subtract rather than add colour. The pivotal learning move is predict-observe-reconcile: a learner predicts and explains an object's colour under coloured light, then watches it change, which refutes colour-as-innate-property. Subtractive reasoning is documented as genuinely hard, and additive light mixing must be kept visibly distinct from subtractive pigment/filter behaviour.
misconceptions: Colour is an innate, fixed property of the object (a red dress 'just is' red), independent of the light illuminating it.
The light merely 'brightens' the object's own colour, rather than the object selecting some frequencies from the light and absorbing the rest.
Colour is ADDED by the light or a filter 'dyes' all light its own colour (adder), rather than SUBTRACTED by selective absorption.
White light is 'just light' / 'normal light', not a mixture of all colours — which undermines both dispersion and colour.
Confusing additive light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow) with subtractive pigment/filter behaviour; e.g. expecting red + green spotlights to make brown (documented 70%+ error).
Believing a prism 'adds' or 'creates' colours, rather than separating colours already present in white light.
Predicting a red object under blue light stays red or looks blue/dark-red, instead of black (no red present to reflect).
Forgetting the whole path — perceived colour is the light REACHING THE EYE, which depends on BOTH the pigment and the illuminating light.

activities.title: Colour lab: drive the light, swap the objects
steps: Before each reveal, write a prediction AND a reason for what colour an object will appear (e.g. 'red apple under a pure blue lamp').

Dial a light source from white to pure red, green, or blue and shine it on a shelf of objects (red apple, white shirt, black cloth, multicoloured toy); observe which wavelengths are absorbed and which reflect back to the eye.
Watch the red apple turn near-black under pure blue light, and the white shirt take on the lamp's colour; reconcile each observation with your prediction.
Split a white beam through a prism into ROYGBIV, then pass the spectrum through a second prism to recombine it back to white.

Compare the subtractive object/filter behaviour with a separate panel showing overlapping red, green and blue spotlights (additive mixing to yellow/cyan/magenta/white), noting the two rules give opposite results.
Pass white light through coloured filters and describe what is transmitted versus absorbed.
activities.insight: Perceived colour is light-and-pigment together, not a fixed property of the object: a surface returns only the colours the light supplies and the surface does not absorb. White light is a mixture a prism separates (not creates), and filters/pigments subtract colour while light sources add.

activities.title: Predict-observe-reconcile with a real coloured lamp
steps: Under normal lighting, note that the object is a bright red; then, in a darkened space and before the coloured lamp is switched on, write down the colour you predict it will appear under a pure blue (or green) LED lamp AND your reason.
Switch on the lamp and observe how the object appears (with a saturated red pigment and a narrow-band blue or green lamp it should look very dark, close to black); compare with your prediction.
Repeat with a WHITE object for comparison and note that it takes on the lamp's colour (blue under a blue lamp, green under a green lamp).
State in your own words why the two objects behave differently.
activities.insight: A discrepant event that colour-as-innate cannot explain: the red object goes near-black because no red light is present to reflect, while the white object reflects whatever colour the lamp provides.

activities.title: Reason about colour: spectrum order, filters, and prisms
steps: Order the visible spectrum by increasing frequency (red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest).
Predict and explain the colour of a red object seen under blue light, and of a white and a black object under the same light.
Match an object plus an illuminating colour to the perceived colour.

Predict what is seen when white light passes through a red filter, and explain why an opaque coloured object behaves like a selective filter, except that it selects the light it reflects rather than the light it transmits.
Predict the result of overlapping red and green spotlights and explain why it is yellow, not brown.
Explain why a prism disperses white light and why a second prism can recombine the spectrum to white.
activities.insight: Consolidate the subtractive model and separate it from additive light mixing, tying colour order to the physical wave property that dispersion sorts.

checkQuestion: A red London bus is parked in a dark garage. I switch on a lamp that gives out ONLY pure blue light — no other colours at all. What colour does the bus look now? And explain WHY it looks that colour.
checkAnswer: It looks BLACK (very dark). A red object looks red because its surface reflects red light and absorbs the others; under pure blue light there is no red for it to reflect, and it absorbs the blue, so almost no light comes off it to our eyes — it appears black.
